query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount (~0.3 at.%) of zirconium (Zr) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy will stabilize the lamellar interfaces through grain‐boundary segregation and coherent nano‐precipitate formation. This in turn will simultaneously enhance strength, ductility, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations and long‐term mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy whose as‐cast mechanical properties (strength and ductility) and creep/corrosion resistance are below industrial requirements for fastener applications.
generation.intervention: A single microalloying intervention by adding approximately 0.3 atomic percent zirconium during melting, aiming to preserve the lamellar structure while modifying the chemistry at phase boundaries.
generation.conditions: The intervention is targeted for fastener components meant to operate under cyclic thermal fluctuations (approximately –50°C to 700°C), under continuous mechanical loading at room temperature (with suppression of creep over long durations) and in corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing media). Laboratory testing should mimic these conditions to assess performance improvements.
generation.structural_mediator: Zr is expected to segregate at lamellar interfaces and grain boundaries, leading to the formation of coherent or semi‐coherent Zr‐rich nano-precipitates. These features act as dislocation pinning centers and stabilize the microstructure, enhancing both the mechanical and corrosion protective characteristics.
generation.mechanism: By introducing Zr, the alloy's internal interfaces become fortified against dislocation motion and boundary migration. This results in improved yield strength and work hardening (benefiting ductility) while also reducing creep by impeding boundary sliding. Simultaneously, Zr can enhance the quality of the passive film by forming stable Zr oxides at the surface, thereby improving corrosion resistance under aggressive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the Zr-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit roughly a 15–20% increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths, improved ductility due to delayed crack initiation through enhanced work hardening, a lower room-temperature creep rate, and a reduced corrosion rate under cyclic thermal and corrosive conditions, all while retaining the uniform lamellar microstructure.
generation.baseline: The unmodified, uniform fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy processed by conventional methods as reported in the literature.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected provided that the Zr addition remains at a trace level (~0.3 at.%) so as not to disrupt the lamellar morphology. The improvements are anticipated within operating temperatures between –50°C and 700°C, under mechanical loading and room-temperature creep testing durations representative of long-term service, and in corrosive media representative of industrial fastener exposures.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on the evidence that microalloying can stabilize phase boundaries and improve corrosion resistance (PMC6353877::web::018::discussion and PMC10488378::web::000::abstract) and extends these findings by proposing that Zr—unexplored in the current EHEA literature map—can provide multifaceted enhancements. The exact quantitative improvements and optimal Zr content remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples using identical processing routes to achieve the fine lamellar microstructure. One group will include a 0.3 at.% Zr addition; the control group will have no Zr. Subject both groups to: (a) cyclic thermal fatigue experiments covering –50°C to 700°C, (b) extended room-temperature creep tests, and (c) electrochemical and immersion corrosion tests in chloride-containing solutions. Mechanical properties (tensile properties, creep rate) will also be measured under standard conditions.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile tests (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Creep tests (creep strain rate and time-to-failure)
Cyclic thermal fatigue testing (number of cycles to crack initiation, crack propagation behavior)
Electrochemical corrosion tests (corrosion current density, passivation behavior, weight loss over time)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped specimens do not show statistically significant improvements—defined as less than a 5% improvement in mechanical properties, creep resistance, and corrosion performance compared to the control group—then the hypothesis should be rejected.

The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
